article.Citation: Barrett SP, Archambault J, Engelberg MJ, Pihl RO. Hallucinogenic Drugs Attenuate the Subjective Response to Alcohol in Humans. Human Psychopharmacology: Clinical and Experimental. 1999.
article.Title: Hallucinogenic Drugs Attenuate the Subjective Response to Alcohol in Humans
article.GenderCategory: 19 male, 3 female of 22 total interviewed (Results narrative, spelled out as "Nineteen males and three females"); Table 1's n=17 codable-data subsample comprises 14 male, 3 female

ae_events.Description: One participant volunteered that combining psilocybin with alcohol produced a very unpleasant synergistic effect

article.IsObservational: Retrospective, self-report structured-interview study using snowball sampling to characterize naturalistic/recreational co-use of alcohol with LSD or psilocybin. No randomization, no researcher-administered drug protocol -- participants are describing past personal drug-use experiences. Classified as observational (naturalistic/retrospective self-report), not an RCT or interventional design.
article.N: Genuine internal inconsistency in the article, not an OCR/font-encoding artifact: Methods states (in cleanly decodable text -- ligatures/punctuation only, digits unaffected) 'Of the 14 individuals contacted, three declined to participate, leaving a final sample of 11 subjects.' Results separately states, in plain spelled-out English words with no font-encoding involved, 'Nineteen males and three females were interviewed for the present study' (19+3=22). These cannot both be the same figure. I did not construct any digit-substitution/cipher theory to reconcile them (per instructions). Instead I cross-checked against a third, independently legible source: Table 1 contains exactly 17 subject rows, of which exactly 3 are coded female (subjects H, R, S) and 14 male. Results states 4 subjects were excluded entirely from interaction analysis (no intoxicating alcohol+drug co-use) plus 1 excluded for uncodable responses = 5 excluded. 22 (19M+3F) minus 5 excluded = 17, matching Table 1's row count exactly, and the female count (3) matches exactly between Results and Table 1, consistent with all 5 exclusions having been male (19-5=14, matching Table 1's male count). This three-way arithmetic convergence (spelled-out Results total, Table 1 row count, Table 1 gender counts) supports 22 as the total interviewed/enrolled sample, with 'final sample of 11' in Methods appearing to be an error inconsistent with the rest of the article. I report N=22 as the enrolled/interviewed sample; note that only 17 of these 22 had codable data for the primary LSD-alcohol comparison (fewer still for some psilocybin sub-analyses), so N should be read as enrolled rather than uniformly analyzed. Flagging for human review given the unresolved Methods discrepancy.
article.PctFemale: 3/22 = 13.6%, using N=22 per the reasoning above (3 females stated explicitly in Results and independently corroborated by Table 1's 3 female rows).
article.GenderCategory: See N rationale -- Results narrative (22 total: 19M/3F) and Table 1 subsample (17 total: 14M/3F) both reported to preserve the discrepancy rather than collapsing it.
article.AE_denominator: The article never frames the single reported adverse subjective experience as part of a systematic safety assessment with a stated denominator (e.g., 'X of Y participants reported...'). All 22 interviewed participants were asked open-ended questions that could in principle have surfaced such an experience, but since no explicit assessed-denominator is stated, coded 'Not numbered' rather than assuming 22.
article.ArmScope: Single-group naturalistic/retrospective survey with no non-exposed comparator arm -- entire sample is psychedelic-(LSD/psilocybin)-exposed by definition of the recruitment criteria (past co-use of alcohol and LSD and/or psilocybin).
article.SafetyReported: The study was not designed to systematically assess AEs/safety (its aim was characterizing subjective drug-interaction effects via Likert ratings). However, Results incidentally reports one participant's spontaneously volunteered 'very unpleasant synergistic effect' from combining psilocybin and alcohol, which is a safety-relevant event; per the cardinal safety-dataset principle (understating harm is the worse error), this is coded as SafetyReported=Y / AnyAEReported=Y with 1 distinct AE rather than treated as absent.
article.PctBIPOC: Race/ethnicity not reported anywhere in the article.
article.Corpus/Prefix: No substance/condition grouping label evident within the article text itself.
article.GeneralNote_UnrelatedNumericAnomalies: Several other numeric strings in the article (e.g., the journal volume rendered as '04' rather than '14', and Discussion subgroup counts such as '04 LSD users' / '02 reported a complete blockade') show digit patterns that also look inconsistent with known correct values, distinct from the clean ligature/punctuation substitutions (fi->_, ff->}, fl->~, comma->\, period->[) that were straightforward to read through. Per the input-fidelity instructions, no decoding rule was constructed for these; since none of them map to a schema field (they concern LSD/psilocybin sub-analysis breakdowns not captured by this schema), they were left unresolved and do not affect any extracted value.

ae_events.Barrett 1999_AE01: Description is under-specified: authors give no detail on duration, functional impact, or whether any intervention occurred (unsurprising given this is a retrospective account of a past recreational event with no clinical monitoring infrastructure) -- graded Mild by default per the rubric's under-specified-AE rule, SeverityIndeterminate=Y. Classified as challenging_experience rather than AE/both since it is subjective/in-session phenomenology from naturalistic combined use, not a clinically observed/managed event, and CEQ-sense challenging experiences are not to be silently folded into a clinical AE count. InterventionRequired=N because the naturalistic community-use setting had no clinical intervention capability/context (retrospective self-report of past personal use, not a monitored session) -- article does not describe any intervention and none was structurally possible. A separate mention by another participant of feeling 'a little bloated' after heavy drinking on LSD (representative-reports section) was not coded as a distinct AE: it is presented as a mundane, non-adverse sensation consistent with ordinary alcohol consumption rather than a notable challenging or adverse effect.
